note.text: Resistance could arise from defence of sovereignty, land, livelihoods, religion and social institutions. Taxes, labour demands and interference in established authority could provoke opposition. Different communities faced different pressures, so there was no single universal cause. Resistance also took different forms, from armed action to petitions, refusal and evasion. Explaining causes requires linking a demand or change to the interests it threatened and to the response that followed.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: Resistance could arise from defence of sovereignty, land, livelihoods, religion and social institutions. Taxes, labour demands and interference in established authority could provoke opposition. Different communities faced different pressures, so there was no single universal cause. Resistance also took different forms, from armed action to petitions, refusal and evasion. Explaining causes requires linking a demand or change to the interests it threatened and to the response that followed.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: A demand for land may threaten farming and political authority at once. An imposed labour requirement may remove workers from household production. A religious or cultural interference may be experienced as an attack on community institutions. These categories help organise evidence but should not replace the detailed story of a named resistance movement.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Distinguish long-term grievances from an immediate trigger. Avoid calling resistance irrational merely because an official record labels it rebellion. Ask whose authority and livelihood were affected, and compare the accounts of those imposing and those opposing a demand.
